title: The True Meaning of Power
gist: David Sacks (CFR Senior Fellow for Asia Studies, not the tech investor) argues the second Trump administration misreads Hans Morgenthau's realism: Morgenthau saw power as a psychological relationship based on consent that must be tamed by morality and bound to purpose, whereas Trump equates power with force—Iran, Venezuela/Maduro, Cuba blockade, Caribbean strikes, threats to Canada and Denmark—making him a 'Machiavelli without virtù' whose overreach, like Vietnam, will erode the domestic foundations of American power.

insights.claim: The author lists the second Trump administration's uses of force as striking boats in the Caribbean, kidnapping Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, blockading Cuba, and waging war on Iran, plus threatening military action against allies Canada and Denmark.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: A multi-theater pattern of U.S. force in the Western Hemisphere and Middle East is a persistent geopolitical risk factor.
insights.quote: striking boats in the Caribbean, kidnapping Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, blockading Cuba, and waging war on Iran

insights.claim: The Trump administration did not seek congressional authorization for the war in Iran and refused even to make the case to the American people before striking.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Unilateral war initiation increases the risk of sudden escalation without political warning.
insights.quote: the administration not only failed to seek congressional authorization for the war in Iran, but it also refused to even make the case to the American people before striking

insights.claim: White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in January invoked the 'iron laws of the world,' one governed by strength, force, and power, typifying the administration's outlook; the administration labels its approach 'flexible realism.'
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Officials' explicit force-centric doctrine implies continued willingness to use military power.

insights.claim: The author argues Russia's sphere-of-influence push in Eastern Europe, China's quest for hegemony in East Asia, and the U.S. revival of the Monroe Doctrine in the Western Hemisphere all reflect the primacy of national interests over norms.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: A spheres-of-influence world implies regionalized blocs and higher geopolitical risk premia.

insights.claim: The author, channeling Morgenthau, argues real power lies in the ability to influence other countries through consent rather than coercion, so the use of force signifies the abdication of political power rather than its culmination.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Frequent U.S. use of force may signal declining, not rising, influence—relevant to dollar and alliance-based assets.
insights.quote: In this view, the use of force signifies the abdication of political power rather than its culmination.

insights.claim: The author contends the Trump administration's acts of aggression are confessions of its inability to shape events through other means.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Reads escalation as weakness; expect allies to defer less to U.S. prerogatives.
insights.quote: its acts of aggression around the world are confessions of its inability to shape events through other means

insights.claim: When the U.S. limits its own power, abides by norms and consults allies, others find American influence more palatable, which sustains it; untethered from restraints, others will stop deferring and the world becomes more dangerous.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Erosion of allied deference is a mechanism for long-run decline in U.S. geopolitical leverage.
insights.quote: if Washington’s actions become untethered from these restraints, others will no longer defer to American prerogatives, and the world will become a more dangerous place

insights.claim: The author applies Morgenthau's verdict on E. H. Carr to Trump: a 'Machiavelli without virtù,' playing power politics without skill or judgment and leading his country to disaster.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Framing of U.S. policy as high-miscalculation-risk in an era with thin margins for error.
insights.quote: It is a disastrous thing to be a Machiavelli without virtù

insights.claim: Morgenthau held that superior power gives no moral or legal right to do all that power is physically capable of, whereas the Trump administration seems to believe not using available power is wasting it.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: An administration that sees unused power as waste is predisposed to further interventions.
insights.quote: “superior power gives no right, either moral or legal, to do with that power all that it is physically capable of doing.”

insights.claim: The author argues analysts who root Trump's actions in realism, such as a New York Times Magazine essay titled 'The Theory That Gives Trump a Blank Check for Aggression,' misread the tradition, because realism without its moral dimension is mistaken and dangerous.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Intellectual contest over 'realism' shapes elite justification for or against U.S. interventions.

insights.claim: Morgenthau's Politics Among Nations became the most widely adopted international relations textbook in the U.S. and argued only a balance of power, not disarmament, collective security or international law, could contain the struggle for power.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Balance-of-power logic implies alliances and regional deterrence matter more than institutions.
insights.quote: Power could be tamed only by countervailing power.

insights.claim: Morgenthau observed that moral restraints historically stigmatized once-common practices like assassinating rival leaders or killing large shares of civilian populations, making them normally impossible to execute.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Erosion of such norms (e.g., leader seizures) lowers the threshold for extreme state actions.

insights.claim: Morgenthau argued a nation must pursue its interests for a transcendent purpose; for the U.S., that purpose lay in its democracy and civic life, serving 'as a light to attract strangers, not as a flame to be spread throughout the world.'
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Domestic democratic health is framed as the wellspring of U.S. international power.
insights.quote: “as a light to attract strangers, not as a flame to be spread throughout the world.”

insights.claim: Morgenthau warned as early as 1961 that Vietnam could become a quagmire like France's war in Algeria and rejected the domino theory on realist grounds, arguing a communist Vietnam would not shift Asia's balance of power.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Historical template for realists opposing wars of choice—analogous arguments now apply to Iran.

insights.claim: The author argues Vietnam showed that misadventures abroad can boomerang, weakening American democracy and societal cohesion and ultimately the country's international standing.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Foreign wars carry domestic political and social costs that feed back into U.S. stability.
insights.quote: Vietnam showed that misadventures abroad could boomerang, weakening American democracy and societal cohesion

insights.claim: The author says the Trump administration's attacks on the courts, the press, and universities are intertwined with its aggressive foreign policy and are undermining the foundations of American power, making U.S. democracy a cautionary tale.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Institutional erosion is a slow-burn risk to U.S. soft power and its institutional premium.
insights.quote: American democracy, far from serving as “a light to attract strangers,” is fast becoming a cautionary tale.

insights.claim: The author warns the U.S. faces an era of intensified great-power competition in which the margin for error is thin and the cost of miscalculation could be catastrophic.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Tail-risk framing for great-power conflict; supports hedges against geopolitical shocks.
insights.quote: an era of intensified great-power competition, one in which the margin for error is thin and the cost of miscalculation could be catastrophic
insights.locator: Returning to the foundations of realism

insights.claim: The author concludes the United States has lost its purpose and that unless it rediscovers it, discrete foreign policy successes will be irrelevant.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Tactical wins may mask strategic decline in U.S. influence.
insights.quote: The United States has lost its purpose, and unless it rediscovers it, discrete foreign policy successes will be irrelevant.

insights.claim: Morgenthau, a German Jewish refugee from Coburg—the first town to elect the Nazis—concluded from watching Weimar judges that 'what was decisive was not the merits of different legal interpretations but the distribution of political power.'
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Context for why institutions fail when power shifts—relevant to judging durability of legal checks.
insights.quote: “what was decisive was not the merits of different legal interpretations but the distribution of political power.”

insights.claim: Morgenthau believed Western democracies' blind faith in international law and the League of Nations, born of misunderstanding human nature, led to appeasement of Hitler.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Realist skepticism of institutions cuts both ways: neither naive legalism nor unchecked force works.
